source: AIEEE 2003
question: \[ \text{Evaluate } I=\int_0^1 x(1-x)^n\,dx \]
solution: This is exactly the Beta integral \(B(2,n+1)=\dfrac{1!\,n!}{(n+2)!}\). Since \((n+2)!=(n+2)(n+1)\cdot n!\), it simplifies to \(\dfrac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)}\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Any \(\int_0^1 x^m(1-x)^n dx\) is \(\dfrac{m!\,n!}{(m+n+1)!}\) — don't binomially expand \((1-x)^n\) by hand.
subject: math

source: AIEEE 2002
question: \[ \int_0^{2} [x^2]\,dx \]
solution: \(x^2\) crosses each integer at \(x=1,\sqrt2,\sqrt3,2\). So \([x^2]=0\) on \([0,1)\), \(1\) on \([1,\sqrt2)\), \(2\) on \([\sqrt2,\sqrt3)\), \(3\) on \([\sqrt3,2)\).\n        \[ I = 1\cdot(\sqrt2-1)+2\cdot(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)+3\cdot(2-\sqrt3) = 5-\sqrt2-\sqrt3 \]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: With \([f(x)]\) inside an integral, first solve \(f(x)=\)integer to find every breakpoint, then treat each piece as a constant.
subject: math

source: JEE Main 2018 (Offline)
question: \[ \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \frac{\sin^2 x}{1+2^{x}}\,dx \]
solution: Add the integral to its own \(x\to-x\) copy:\n        \[ 2I=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\sin^2x\left(\frac1{1+2^x}+\frac1{1+2^{-x}}\right)dx \]\n        The bracket collapses to \(1\) (since \(\frac1{1+2^{-x}}=\frac{2^x}{1+2^x}\)), leaving \(2I=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\sin^2x\,dx\), an even integrand. So \(I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2x\,dx=\dfrac\pi4\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\dfrac{1}{1+a^x}+\dfrac{1}{1+a^{-x}}=1\) for any base \(a\) — the standard move whenever an exponential with no obvious antiderivative sits in the denominator over a symmetric interval.
subject: math

source: AIEEE 2011
question: \[ \int_0^1 \frac{8\ln(1+x)}{1+x^2}\,dx \]
solution: Substitute \(x=\tan\theta\): the integral becomes \(8\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\ln(1+\tan\theta)\,d\theta\). Let \(\theta\to\frac\pi4-\theta\): \(\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\theta\right)=\dfrac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}\), so \(1+\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\theta\right)=\dfrac{2}{1+\tan\theta}\). Adding the two forms of the inner integral gives \(2J=\dfrac\pi4\ln2\), so \(J=\dfrac\pi8\ln2\), and the answer is \(8J=\pi\ln2\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}dx\) is the standard cue for \(x=\tan\theta\) — try that substitution first and see whether the result is a King's-rule integral in disguise.
subject: math

source: AIEEE 2002
question: \[ \int_0^{10\pi} |\sin x|\,dx \]
solution: \(|\sin x|\) has period \(\pi\), and \(\int_0^\pi \sin x\,dx=2\) (since \(\sin x\ge0\) there). So \(\int_0^{10\pi}|\sin x|\,dx=10\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\sin x\,dx=20\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(|\sin x|\) and \(|\cos x|\) are \(\pi\)-periodic, not \(2\pi\)-periodic — using the smaller period cuts the work in half.
subject: math

source: JEE Main 2015 (Offline)
question: \[ \int_2^4 \frac{\log(x^2)}{\log(x^2)+\log(36-12x+x^2)}\,dx \]
solution: Notice \(36-12x+x^2=(6-x)^2\), so the integrand is \(f(x)=\dfrac{\log(x^2)}{\log(x^2)+\log((6-x)^2)}\). With \(a=2,\ b=4\), the King's-rule partner is \(a+b-x=6-x\): \(f(6-x)=\dfrac{\log((6-x)^2)}{\log((6-x)^2)+\log(x^2)}=1-f(x)\). Adding \(I=\int f\) and \(I=\int f(6-x)=\int(1-f)\) gives \(2I=\int_2^4 1\,dx=2\), so \(I=1\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Whenever the denominator is the numerator plus a King's-rule-shifted twin, \(f(x)+f(a+b-x)\) is what you should compute first — here it's exactly \(1\).
subject: math

source: JEE Main 2021 (26th February Morning Shift)
question: \[ \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \frac{\cos^2 x}{1+3^{x}}\,dx \]
solution: Same trick as the \(2^x\) version: add the integral to its \(x\to-x\) copy. The bracket \(\frac1{1+3^x}+\frac1{1+3^{-x}}\) collapses to \(1\), leaving \(2I=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^2x\,dx\). So \(I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2x\,dx=\dfrac\pi4\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: The base of the exponential (2, 3, or any \(a>0\)) never matters for this trick — only that \(\frac1{1+a^x}+\frac1{1+a^{-x}}=1\).
subject: math

source: JEE Main 2013 (Offline)
question: \[ \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \frac{dx}{1+\sqrt{\tan x}} \]
solution: Let \(x\to\frac{\pi}{6}+\frac{\pi}{3}-x=\frac\pi2-x\): \(\tan\left(\frac\pi2-x\right)=\cot x=\dfrac1{\tan x}\), so \(1+\sqrt{\tan(\frac\pi2-x)}=1+\dfrac1{\sqrt{\tan x}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{\tan x}+1}{\sqrt{\tan x}}\). Adding the original integrand \(\frac1{1+\sqrt{\tan x}}\) to this transformed one gives exactly \(1\), so \(2I=\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}1\,dx=\dfrac\pi6\), giving \(I=\dfrac\pi{12}\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: When you see \(\dfrac1{1+\sqrt{g(x)}}\), check whether King's rule turns \(g(x)\) into \(1/g(x)\) — that's exactly what makes the two copies add to \(1\).
subject: math

source: AIEEE 2005
question: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(f(2)=6\) and \(f'(2)=\dfrac1{48}\). Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to2}\frac{1}{x-2}\int_6^{f(x)} 4t^3\,dt\).
solution: The antiderivative of \(4t^3\) is \(t^4\), so the integral equals \(f(x)^4-6^4=f(x)^4-1296\). As \(x\to2\), both this and \(x-2\) go to \(0\), so apply L'Hôpital: differentiate the numerator using the chain rule (FTC), \(\frac{d}{dx}\left[f(x)^4-1296\right]=4f(x)^3f'(x)\). At \(x=2\): \(4\cdot6^3\cdot\dfrac1{48}=4\cdot216\cdot\dfrac1{48}=18\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: A variable upper limit inside a 0/0 limit is almost always solved by evaluating the integral's antiderivative first, then differentiating — don't try to compute the integral directly.
subject: math

source: IIT-JEE 1985
question: \[ \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{x\sin x\cos x}{\cos^4 x+\sin^4 x}\,dx \]
solution: Swap \(x\to\frac\pi2-x\): the denominator is unchanged, giving \(2I=\dfrac\pi2\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sin x\cos x}{\sin^4x+\cos^4x}dx\). Using \(\sin^4x+\cos^4x=1-\tfrac12\sin^22x\) and \(u=\cos2x\), that integral evaluates to \(\dfrac\pi4\). So \(2I=\dfrac\pi2\cdot\dfrac\pi4=\dfrac{\pi^2}{8}\), giving \(I=\dfrac{\pi^2}{16}\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\sin^4x+\cos^4x=1-\frac12\sin^22x\) is worth memorizing — it turns messy quartic denominators into a single \(\sin2x\) term.
subject: math

source: IIT-JEE 2006
question: Find the value of \(5050\,\dfrac{I_1}{I_2}\), where \(I_1=\displaystyle\int_0^1(1-x^{50})^{100}dx\) and \(I_2=\displaystyle\int_0^1(1-x^{50})^{101}dx\).
solution: Let \(u=x^{50}\); this is a Beta-family ratio in disguise. Integrating \(I_1\) by parts (peeling off one factor of \((1-x^{50})\) and using \(x=x\)) produces a reduction relation between consecutive \(I_n\)'s of exactly this type, giving \(\dfrac{I_1}{I_2}=\dfrac{5051}{5050}\). So \(5050\cdot\dfrac{5051}{5050}=5051\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Ratios of the form \(\int_0^1(1-x^k)^n dx\) for consecutive \(n\) are reduction-formula problems — the algebra is identical in spirit to \(I_n=\int\tan^nx\,dx\), just with a different building block.
subject: math

source: IIT-JEE 1998
question: Given that \(\displaystyle\int_0^1\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac1{1-x+x^2}\right)dx=2\int_0^1\tan^{-1}x\,dx\), evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^1\tan^{-1}(1-x+x^2)\,dx\).
solution: Since \(1-x+x^2>0\) for all real \(x\), \(\tan^{-1}(1-x+x^2)+\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac1{1-x+x^2}\right)=\dfrac\pi2\). Integrating over \([0,1]\) and using the given identity:\n        \[ \int_0^1\tan^{-1}(1-x+x^2)dx = \frac\pi2 - 2\int_0^1\tan^{-1}x\,dx \]\n        Since \(\int_0^1\tan^{-1}x\,dx=\left[x\tan^{-1}x-\tfrac12\ln(1+x^2)\right]_0^1=\dfrac\pi4-\dfrac12\ln2\), the answer is \(\dfrac\pi2-\left(\dfrac\pi2-\ln2\right)=\ln2\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\tan^{-1}A+\tan^{-1}(1/A)=\frac\pi2\) for \(A>0\) turns a hard \(\tan^{-1}\) integral into a known one — look for a positive expression paired with its reciprocal.
subject: math

source: IIT-JEE 2001 Screening
question: For \(a>0\), evaluate \[ \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \frac{\cos^2 x}{1+a^{x}}\,dx \]
solution: Add the integral to its \(x\to-x\) copy: \(2I=\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos^2x\left(\dfrac1{1+a^x}+\dfrac1{1+a^{-x}}\right)dx=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos^2x\,dx\), since the bracket collapses to \(1\) regardless of \(a\). So \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\cos^2x\,dx=\dfrac\pi2\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: This \(1/(1+a^x)\) symmetry trick works for any positive base \(a\) — the answer never depends on \(a\) at all.
subject: math

source: IIT-JEE 1993
question: \[ \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{dx}{1+\tan^3 x} \]
solution: Let \(x\to\frac\pi2-x\): \(\tan\left(\frac\pi2-x\right)=\cot x\), so the transformed integrand is \(\dfrac1{1+\cot^3x}=\dfrac{\tan^3x}{\tan^3x+1}\). Adding this to the original integrand \(\dfrac1{1+\tan^3x}\) gives exactly \(1\). So \(2I=\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx=\dfrac\pi2\), giving \(I=\dfrac\pi4\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\dfrac1{1+g(x)}\) paired with \(\dfrac1{1+1/g(x)}\) always sums to \(1\) — recognize this shape before trying to integrate \(\tan^3x\) directly.
subject: math

source: IIT-JEE 1994
question: \[ \int_2^3 \frac{\sqrt x}{\sqrt{5-x}+\sqrt x}\,dx \]
solution: This is the f/(f+f∘shift) trick with \(a=2,\,b=3\), so \(a+b-x=5-x\) and \(f(x)=\sqrt x\). Directly: \(I=\dfrac{b-a}2=\dfrac{3-2}2=\dfrac12\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Whenever the denominator is \(f(x)+f(a+b-x)\) for the exact interval \([a,b]\), the integral is just \((b-a)/2\) — no algebra needed at all.
subject: math

source: IIT-JEE 1999
question: \[ \int_{\pi/4}^{3\pi/4} \frac{dx}{1+\cos x} \]
solution: Use \(1+\cos x=2\cos^2(x/2)\), so the integrand is \(\dfrac12\sec^2(x/2)\), whose antiderivative is \(\tan(x/2)\). Evaluating: \(\left[\tan\dfrac x2\right]_{\pi/4}^{3\pi/4}=\tan\dfrac{3\pi}8-\tan\dfrac\pi8=(1+\sqrt2)-(\sqrt2-1)=2\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(1+\cos x=2\cos^2(x/2)\) and \(1-\cos x=2\sin^2(x/2)\) turn awkward \(1\pm\cos x\) denominators into a clean \(\sec^2\) or \(\csc^2\) form.
subject: math

source: IIT-JEE 1997
question: \[ \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \frac{2x(1+\sin x)}{1+\cos^2 x}\,dx \]
solution: Split into \(\dfrac{2x}{1+\cos^2x}+\dfrac{2x\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}\). The first term is odd (odd \(\times\) even) so it vanishes over \([-\pi,\pi]\). The second term is even, so \(I=2\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\dfrac{2x\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}dx\). Apply King's rule (\(x\to\pi-x\)) to that piece to strip off the lone \(x\), reducing it to \(2\pi\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}dx\) minus itself; solving gives \(\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\dfrac{x\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}dx=\dfrac{\pi^2}4\), so the full answer is \(4\times\dfrac{\pi^2}4=\pi^2\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Split a mixed integrand into an odd piece (which vanishes) and an even piece first — it's often much less work than applying King's rule to the whole expression at once.
subject: math

source: JEE Advanced 2016 Paper 2
question: \[ \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \frac{x^2\cos x}{1+e^x}\,dx \]
solution: Add the integral to its \(x\to-x\) copy: \(2I=\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}x^2\cos x\left(\dfrac1{1+e^x}+\dfrac1{1+e^{-x}}\right)dx=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}x^2\cos x\,dx\), an even integrand. So \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}x^2\cos x\,dx\). Integrating by parts twice: \(\left[x^2\sin x+2x\cos x-2\sin x\right]_0^{\pi/2}=\dfrac{\pi^2}4-2\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: The \(1/(1+e^x)\) symmetry trick works with any even function multiplying it, no matter how complicated — it just needs one round of integration by parts afterward.
subject: math

source: BITSAT 2025
question: \[ \int_0^{\pi} \ln(\sin x)\,dx \]
solution: Let \(x\to\pi-x\): \(\sin(\pi-x)=\sin x\), so King's rule alone doesn't simplify it directly — instead split at \(\pi/2\) and substitute \(x\to\pi-x\) on the second half to show both halves equal \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin x)dx\). Then use \(\sin x=2\sin(x/2)\cos(x/2)\) to relate \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin x)dx\) to itself plus a \(\ln2\) term, giving \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin x)dx=-\dfrac\pi2\ln2\). Doubling: \(\int_0^\pi\ln(\sin x)dx=-\pi\ln2\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin x)dx=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\cos x)dx=-\frac\pi2\ln2\) is a famous standard result — memorize it rather than re-deriving it under time pressure.
subject: math

source: BITSAT 2024
question: \[ \int_0^{\infty} \frac{dx}{(x^2+a^2)(x^2+b^2)} \quad (a\neq b) \]
solution: Partial fractions: \(\dfrac1{(x^2+a^2)(x^2+b^2)}=\dfrac1{b^2-a^2}\left(\dfrac1{x^2+a^2}-\dfrac1{x^2+b^2}\right)\). Each piece integrates to a \(\tan^{-1}\) form: \(\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\dfrac{dx}{x^2+a^2}=\dfrac\pi{2a}\). So the answer is \(\dfrac1{b^2-a^2}\left(\dfrac\pi{2a}-\dfrac\pi{2b}\right)=\dfrac\pi{2ab(a+b)}\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\int_0^\infty\frac{dx}{x^2+c^2}=\frac{\pi}{2c}\) is worth memorizing outright — it turns this whole problem into partial fractions plus substitution.
subject: math

source: BITSAT 2024
question: \[ \int_0^{\pi/2} \ln(\tan x)\,dx \]
solution: Let \(x\to\frac\pi2-x\): \(\tan\left(\frac\pi2-x\right)=\cot x=\dfrac1{\tan x}\), so \(\ln(\tan(\frac\pi2-x))=-\ln(\tan x)\). This means \(I=-I\), which forces \(I=0\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Whenever King's rule turns the integrand into its exact negative, the answer is \(0\) without any further work.
subject: math

source: BITSAT 2021
question: \[ \int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+x)}{1+x^2}\,dx \]
solution: Substitute \(x=\tan\theta\): the integral becomes \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\ln(1+\tan\theta)\,d\theta\). Let \(\theta\to\frac\pi4-\theta\): \(1+\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\theta\right)=\dfrac2{1+\tan\theta}\). Adding the two forms gives \(2I=\dfrac\pi4\ln2\), so \(I=\dfrac\pi8\ln2\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: This exact integral shows up across multiple boards and years — recognizing \(x=\tan\theta\) followed by King's rule turns it into a two-line solution.
subject: math

source: BITSAT 2020
question: \[ \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{dx}{\tan x+\cot x+\csc x+\sec x} \]
solution: Simplify the denominator: \(\tan x+\cot x=\dfrac1{\sin x\cos x}\) and \(\sec x+\csc x=\dfrac{\sin x+\cos x}{\sin x\cos x}\), so the whole expression is \(\dfrac{1+\sin x+\cos x}{\sin x\cos x}\), making the integrand \(\dfrac{\sin x\cos x}{1+\sin x+\cos x}\). The Weierstrass substitution \(t=\tan(x/2)\) turns this into \(\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{2t(1-t)}{(1+t^2)^2}dt\), which evaluates to \(1-\dfrac\pi4\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Whenever \(\tan x,\cot x,\sec x,\csc x\) all appear together, simplify to a single fraction in \(\sin x,\cos x\) first — it usually collapses into something the Weierstrass substitution can handle cleanly.
subject: math

source: KCET 2021
question: If \(I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^n x\,dx\) for positive integer \(n\), find \(I_{10}+I_8\).
solution: For any \(n\ge2\): \(I_n+I_{n-2}=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^{n-2}x(\tan^2x+1)\,dx=\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^{n-2}x\sec^2x\,dx=\left[\dfrac{\tan^{n-1}x}{n-1}\right]_0^{\pi/4}=\dfrac1{n-1}\). Taking \(n=10\): \(I_{10}+I_8=\dfrac1{9}\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: If a question asks for \(I_n+I_{n-2}\) rather than \(I_n\) alone, derive the one-line recursion \(\frac1{n-1}\) instead of computing either integral outright.
subject: math

source: KCET 2021
question: \[ \int_0^{4042} \frac{\sqrt x}{\sqrt x+\sqrt{4042-x}}\,dx \]
solution: This is the f/(f+f∘shift) trick with \(a=0,\,b=4042\) and \(f(x)=\sqrt x\), since \(a+b-x=4042-x\). Directly: \(I=\dfrac{b-a}2=\dfrac{4042}2=2021\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Large, ugly-looking numbers like 4042 are often a disguise for \(2\times2021\) — check whether the denominator is \(f(x)+f(a+b-x)\) before reaching for a substitution.
subject: math

source: KCET 2020
question: \[ \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \frac{\cos x}{1+e^{x}}\,dx \]
solution: Add the integral to its \(x\to-x\) copy: \(2I=\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos x\left(\dfrac1{1+e^x}+\dfrac1{1+e^{-x}}\right)dx=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos x\,dx=2\). So \(I=1\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\dfrac1{1+e^x}+\dfrac1{1+e^{-x}}=1\) is the single identity behind most \(1/(1+e^x)\)-type integrals over symmetric intervals.
subject: math

source: KCET 2019
question: \[ \int_{-3}^{3} \cot^{-1} x\,dx \]
solution: Since \(\cot^{-1}x\) has range \((0,\pi)\), \(\cot^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}(-x)=\pi\) for all real \(x\). Pairing \(x\) with \(-x\) over the symmetric interval: \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^3\left[\cot^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}(-x)\right]dx=\int_0^3\pi\,dx=3\pi\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\cot^{-1}x\) is not odd (unlike \(\tan^{-1}x\)) because of its range convention — use \(\cot^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}(-x)=\pi\) instead of assuming symmetry cancels it out.
subject: math

source: KCET 2017
question: For positive constants \(a,b\), evaluate \[ \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{dx}{a^2\sin^2 x+b^2\cos^2 x} \]
solution: Divide numerator and denominator by \(\cos^2x\): the integral becomes \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sec^2x\,dx}{a^2\tan^2x+b^2}\). Substitute \(u=\tan x\) (\(u:0\to\infty\)): \(\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\dfrac{du}{a^2u^2+b^2}=\dfrac1{ab}\left[\tan^{-1}\dfrac{au}b\right]_0^\infty=\dfrac1{ab}\cdot\dfrac\pi2=\dfrac\pi{2ab}\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(a^2\sin^2x+b^2\cos^2x\) is a classic \(u=\tan x\) setup — dividing by \(\cos^2x\) turns trig into algebra immediately.
subject: math

source: AP Calculus AB 2022 Free-Response (Q2, adapted)
question: From 5 A.M. to 10 A.M., vehicles arrive at a toll plaza at a rate \(A(t)=450\sin(0.62t)\) vehicles per hour, where \(t\) is hours after 5 A.M. Find the total number of vehicles that arrive from 6 A.M. (\(t=1\)) to 10 A.M. (\(t=5\)).
solution: Total arrivals \(=\displaystyle\int_1^5 450\sin(0.62t)\,dt=\left[-\dfrac{450}{0.62}\cos(0.62t)\right]_1^5\approx1315.897\) vehicles.
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \"Total number that arrive\" over an interval is the definite integral of the rate function — you don't need to solve for a position function first.
subject: math

source: AP Calculus AB 2022 Free-Response (Q2, adapted)
question: Using the toll-plaza arrival rate \(A(t)=450\sin(0.62t)\), find the average rate at which vehicles arrive between 6 A.M. (\(t=1\)) and 10 A.M. (\(t=5\)).
solution: Average value \(=\dfrac1{5-1}\displaystyle\int_1^5 450\sin(0.62t)\,dt\approx\dfrac{1315.897}{4}\approx328.974\) vehicles per hour.
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Average value \(=\dfrac1{b-a}\int_a^b f(t)dt\) reuses the same integral you'd compute for a \"total\" question — just divide by the length of the interval.
subject: math

source: AP Calculus AB 1999 Free-Response Q1 (adapted)
question: A particle moves along the \(x\)-axis with velocity \(v(t)=t\sin(t^2)\) for \(t\ge0\). Find the particle's total displacement from \(t=0\) to \(t=\sqrt\pi\).
solution: Displacement \(=\displaystyle\int_0^{\sqrt\pi} t\sin(t^2)\,dt\). Let \(u=t^2\), \(du=2t\,dt\): \(=\dfrac12\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\sin u\,du=\dfrac12\left[-\cos u\right]_0^\pi=\dfrac12(1-(-1))=1\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: A lone \(t\) multiplying \(\sin(t^2)\) or \(\cos(t^2)\) is the standard cue for \(u=t^2\) — the extra factor of \(t\) is exactly what \(du\) needs.
subject: math

source: AP Calculus AB 2014 Multiple Choice
question: A particle moves along the \(x\)-axis with velocity \(v(t)=\sin(2t)\). If the particle is at \(x=4\) when \(t=0\), find its position when \(t=\pi/2\).
solution: Position \(=4+\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin(2t)\,dt=4+\left[-\dfrac{\cos(2t)}2\right]_0^{\pi/2}=4+\left(\dfrac12+\dfrac12\right)=5\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Position \(=\) initial position \(+\) the definite integral of velocity over the elapsed time — this is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus applied directly to motion.
subject: math

source: BITSAT 2025
question: Express \(\displaystyle\int_a^b e^x\,dx\) as the limit of a Riemann sum, and evaluate it.
solution: Partition \([a,b]\) into \(n\) equal strips of width \(h=\dfrac{b-a}n\), sampling at the right endpoint \(a+rh\): \(\displaystyle\int_a^b e^x dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}h\sum_{r=1}^n e^{a+rh}=\lim_{n\to\infty}he^a\sum_{r=1}^n(e^h)^r\). The inner sum is geometric: \(e^h\dfrac{(e^h)^n-1}{e^h-1}=e^h\dfrac{e^{n h}-1}{e^h-1}\). Since \(nh=b-a\) is fixed, as \(h\to0\) this becomes \(e^a(e^{b-a}-1)\cdot\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{h}{e^h-1}\cdot e^h\to e^a(e^{b-a}-1)=e^b-e^a\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Building a definite integral from its Riemann-sum definition always ends in a geometric series when the integrand is exponential — the limit \(\frac{h}{e^h-1}\to1\) as \(h\to0\) is the key simplification.
subject: math

source: KCET 2022
question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_2^3 x^2\,dx\) as the limit of a sum.
solution: With \(h=\dfrac{3-2}n=\dfrac1n\) and right-endpoint sampling at \(2+rh\): \(\displaystyle\int_2^3 x^2dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}h\sum_{r=1}^n(2+rh)^2=\lim_{n\to\infty}h\sum_{r=1}^n\left(4+4rh+r^2h^2\right)\). Expanding using \(\sum r=\frac{n(n+1)}2\) and \(\sum r^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6\), and taking \(n\to\infty\) with \(h=1/n\), the sum simplifies to \(4+4\left(\dfrac12\right)+\dfrac13=4+2+\dfrac13=\dfrac{19}3\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: For polynomial integrands, expand \((a+rh)^2\) fully and replace \(\sum r\) and \(\sum r^2\) with their closed forms before taking the limit — this matches the antiderivative check \(\left[\frac{x^3}3\right]_2^3=\frac{19}3\).
subject: math

source: Cambridge IGCSE Additional Mathematics (0606) — past paper, Integration topic
question: Find the exact value of \[ \int_2^4 \frac{(x+1)^2}{x^2}\,dx \]
solution: Expand the numerator and divide term by term: \(\dfrac{(x+1)^2}{x^2}=\dfrac{x^2+2x+1}{x^2}=1+\dfrac2x+\dfrac1{x^2}\). The antiderivative is \(x+2\ln x-\dfrac1x\). Evaluating:\n        \[ \left[x+2\ln x-\frac1x\right]_2^4=\left(4+2\ln4-\frac14\right)-\left(2+2\ln2-\frac12\right)=2+2\ln2+\frac14=\ln4+\frac94 \]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Whenever you see a squared bracket over \(x^2\), expand the numerator first — it almost always turns into simple \(x^n\) terms you can integrate directly.
subject: math

source: Cambridge IGCSE Additional Mathematics (0606) — past paper, Integration topic
question: Given that \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos x)=-x\sin x+\cos x\), find the exact value of \[ \int_0^{\pi/6} x\sin x\,dx \]
solution: Rearranging the given derivative: \(x\sin x=\cos x-\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos x)\), so \(\displaystyle\int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x+C\). Evaluating from \(0\) to \(\pi/6\):\n        \[ \left[\sin x-x\cos x\right]_0^{\pi/6}=\left(\frac12-\frac\pi6\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)-(0-0)=\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3\pi}{12} \]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: When a question hands you a derivative you didn't ask for, it's almost always the reverse-product-rule shortcut to the antiderivative you need — rearrange it before reaching for integration by parts.
subject: math

source: Cambridge IGCSE Additional Mathematics (0606) — past paper, Integration topic
question: Find \[ \int_3^5 \left(\frac1{x-1}-\frac1{(x-1)^2}\right)dx \] giving your answer in the form \(a+\ln b\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are rational numbers.
solution: Integrate term by term: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x-1}=\ln|x-1|\) and \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(x-1)^2}=-\frac1{x-1}\). So the antiderivative is \(\ln|x-1|+\dfrac1{x-1}\). Evaluating:\n        \[ \left[\ln|x-1|+\frac1{x-1}\right]_3^5=\left(\ln4+\frac14\right)-\left(\ln2+\frac12\right)=\ln2-\frac14 \]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\dfrac1{(x-1)^2}\) integrates to \(-\dfrac1{x-1}\), not a logarithm — only the power \(-1\) gives a \(\ln\); every other power uses the ordinary power rule.
subject: math

source: Cambridge IGCSE Additional Mathematics (0606) — past paper, Integration topic
question: Find the exact value of \[ \int_0^{\pi/3} \left(\sin\!\left(2x+\frac\pi3\right)-1+\cos 2x\right)dx \]
solution: Integrate each term separately: \(\displaystyle\int\sin\!\left(2x+\tfrac\pi3\right)dx=-\tfrac12\cos\!\left(2x+\tfrac\pi3\right)\), \(\displaystyle\int(-1)dx=-x\), and \(\displaystyle\int\cos2x\,dx=\tfrac12\sin2x\). So the antiderivative is \(-\dfrac12\cos\!\left(2x+\dfrac\pi3\right)-x+\dfrac12\sin2x\). Evaluating from \(0\) to \(\pi/3\):\n        \[ \left(-\frac12\cos\pi-\frac\pi3+\frac12\sin\frac{2\pi}3\right)-\left(-\frac12\cos\frac\pi3-0+0\right)=\left(\frac12-\frac\pi3+\frac{\sqrt3}4\right)-\left(-\frac14\right)=\frac34+\frac{\sqrt3}4-\frac\pi3 \]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Integrate a sum of trig terms one piece at a time — don't try to combine \(\sin(2x+\pi/3)\) and \(\cos2x\) into a single expression before integrating, it's not necessary and easy to get wrong.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^{4\pi} |\cos x|\,dx \]
solution: \(|\cos x|\) has period \(\pi\), and \(\int_0^\pi|\cos x|dx=2\) (two equal lobes of area 1 each). So \(\int_0^{4\pi}|\cos x|dx=4\times2=8\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(|\cos x|\) is \(\pi\)-periodic just like \(|\sin x|\) — always look for the smaller hidden period before integrating directly.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^{6\pi} \sin^2 x\,dx \]
solution: \(\sin^2x\) has period \(\pi\) (not \(2\pi\)), and \(\int_0^\pi\sin^2x\,dx=\dfrac\pi2\). So \(\int_0^{6\pi}\sin^2x\,dx=6\times\dfrac\pi2=3\pi\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Squaring a trig function often halves its period — check \(f(x+\pi)=f(x)\) before assuming the \(2\pi\) period of \(\sin x\) itself applies.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_5^{5+2\pi} \sin x\,dx \]
solution: \(\sin x\) is \(2\pi\)-periodic, and the integral over any full period is always \(0\), regardless of where that period starts. So this integral is \(0\) without any computation.
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\int_a^{a+T}f(x)dx\) is the same for every \(a\) when \(f\) is \(T\)-periodic — for \(\sin x\), that constant value is always \(0\).
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^4 x\,dx \]
solution: Wallis' formula for even \(n=4\): \(\dfrac{3\cdot1}{4\cdot2}\cdot\dfrac\pi2=\dfrac38\cdot\dfrac\pi2=\dfrac{3\pi}{16}\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: For even \(n\), multiply the alternating chain down to \(1\) and finish with \(\times\pi/2\) — no integration required.

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^6 x\,dx \]
solution: Wallis' formula for even \(n=6\): \(\dfrac{5\cdot3\cdot1}{6\cdot4\cdot2}\cdot\dfrac\pi2=\dfrac{15}{48}\cdot\dfrac\pi2=\dfrac{5\pi}{32}\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Remember \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^nx\,dx=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^nx\,dx\) — the formula is identical for either function.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^7 x\,dx \]
solution: Wallis' formula for odd \(n=7\): \(\dfrac{6\cdot4\cdot2}{7\cdot5\cdot3}=\dfrac{48}{105}=\dfrac{16}{35}\) (no \(\pi/2\) factor for odd \(n\)).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Odd powers skip the \(\pi/2\) factor entirely — a common place to lose easy marks by tacking it on out of habit.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^3 x\cos^2 x\,dx \]
solution: Since the power of \(\sin\) is odd, substitute \(u=\cos x\), \(du=-\sin x\,dx\): \(\sin^3x=\sin x(1-\cos^2x)=\sin x(1-u^2)\). The integral becomes \(\displaystyle\int_0^1(1-u^2)u^2\,du=\left[\frac{u^3}3-\frac{u^5}5\right]_0^1=\frac13-\frac15=\frac2{15}\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: When one power is odd, peel off a single factor of that function and substitute for the other — faster than the general Beta formula for small exponents.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^5 x\,dx \]
solution: Wallis' formula for odd \(n=5\): \(\dfrac{4\cdot2}{5\cdot3\cdot1}=\dfrac8{15}\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Write out the alternating chain of integers down to either \(1\) or \(2\) depending on parity — it's faster than substitution for a single power.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: If \(I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^n x\,dx\) satisfies the reduction \(I_n=\dfrac{n-1}nI_{n-2}\), and \(I_6=\dfrac{5\pi}{32}\), find \(I_8\).
solution: Apply the reduction with \(n=8\): \(I_8=\dfrac78I_6=\dfrac78\cdot\dfrac{5\pi}{32}=\dfrac{35\pi}{256}\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Once you're given (or have computed) one \(I_n\), the reduction formula gets you the next one in a single multiplication — no need to re-derive from scratch.

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: If \(I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^n x\,dx\), find \(I_5+I_7\).
solution: Using the standard relation \(I_n+I_{n-2}=\dfrac1{n-1}\) with \(n=7\): \(I_7+I_5=\dfrac16\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: The relation \(I_n+I_{n-2}=\tfrac1{n-1}\) applies for any consecutive-by-2 pair — just plug in the larger index.

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: If \(I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^1 x^n e^{-x}\,dx\) satisfies the reduction \(I_n=nI_{n-1}-e^{-1}\), and \(I_0=1-e^{-1}\), find \(I_1\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Integration by parts on \(x^ne^{-x}\) always produces this style of reduction — one multiplication and one subtraction gets you to the next term.

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: If \(F(t)=\displaystyle\int_t^{2t}e^{tx}\,dx\), find \(F'(0)\) using Leibniz's rule.
solution: \(F'(t)=e^{t(2t)}\cdot2-e^{t\cdot t}\cdot1+\displaystyle\int_t^{2t}xe^{tx}\,dx\). At \(t=0\): the first two terms give \(e^0\cdot2-e^0\cdot1=1\), and the integral's limits both equal \(0\), so it contributes nothing. \(F'(0)=1\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: When evaluating at a specific point, check whether the residual integral's limits coincide there — if so, that term vanishes for free.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: If \(F(t)=\displaystyle\int_0^t (x+t)\,dx\), find \(F'(3)\) using Leibniz's rule.
solution: With \(g(t)=0,\ h(t)=t,\ f(x,t)=x+t\): \(F'(t)=f(t,t)\cdot1-f(0,t)\cdot0+\displaystyle\int_0^t\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}dx=(2t)+\int_0^t1\,dx=2t+t=3t\). At \(t=3\): \(F'(3)=9\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Only the upper limit is variable here, so the lower-limit term of Leibniz's rule drops out — but don't forget the \(\partial f/\partial t\) integral, which still contributes.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: If \(F(t)=\displaystyle\int_t^{t^2}\frac{dx}x\) for \(t>0\), find \(F'(2)\) using Leibniz's rule.
solution: With \(g(t)=t,g'(t)=1,\ h(t)=t^2,h'(t)=2t\), and \(f(x,t)=1/x\) (no explicit \(t\), so \(\partial f/\partial t=0\)): \(F'(t)=\dfrac1{t^2}\cdot2t-\dfrac1t\cdot1=\dfrac2t-\dfrac1t=\dfrac1t\). At \(t=2\): \(F'(2)=\dfrac12\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: If the integrand doesn't explicitly contain the parameter, the \(\partial f/\partial t\) term of Leibniz's rule is automatically zero — only the limit terms survive.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: If \(F(t)=\displaystyle\int_0^t\sin(x-t)\,dx\), find \(F'(\pi/2)\) using Leibniz's rule.
solution: With \(g=0,g'=0,\ h=t,h'=1,\ f(x,t)=\sin(x-t),\ \partial f/\partial t=-\cos(x-t)\): \(F'(t)=\sin(0)\cdot1-0+\displaystyle\int_0^t-\cos(x-t)\,dx=0+\left[-\sin(x-t)\right]_0^t=\sin(-t)=-\sin t\). At \(t=\pi/2\): \(F'(\pi/2)=-1\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Even when the boundary term vanishes (as it does here since \(\sin(t-t)=0\)), you still need to evaluate the residual integral carefully.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: If \(F(t)=\displaystyle\int_0^t xt\,dx\), find \(F'(2)\) using Leibniz's rule.
solution: With \(g=0,g'=0,\ h=t,h'=1,\ f(x,t)=xt,\ \partial f/\partial t=x\): \(F'(t)=(t\cdot t)\cdot1-0+\displaystyle\int_0^t x\,dx=t^2+\frac{t^2}2=\frac{3t^2}2\). At \(t=2\): \(F'(2)=\dfrac{3\cdot4}2=6\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Check your Leibniz-rule answer against direct differentiation when possible: here \(F(t)=t^3/2\) directly, and \(F'(t)=3t^2/2\) matches exactly.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: Express \(\displaystyle\int_0^2 x^3\,dx\) as the limit of a sum, and evaluate it.
solution: With \(h=2/n\) and right-endpoint sampling: \(\displaystyle\int_0^2x^3dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}h\sum_{r=1}^n(rh)^3=\lim_{n\to\infty}h^4\sum_{r=1}^n r^3\). Using \(\sum r^3=\left(\frac{n(n+1)}2\right)^2\) and \(h=2/n\), this simplifies to \(4\), matching \(\left[\frac{x^4}4\right]_0^2=4\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: For \(x^3\), you'll need the closed form \(\sum r^3=\left(\frac{n(n+1)}2\right)^2\) — substitute it in before taking the \(n\to\infty\) limit, not after.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: Express \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 (3x^2+2x)\,dx\) as the limit of a sum, and evaluate it.
solution: With \(h=1/n\): \(\displaystyle\int_0^1(3x^2+2x)dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}h\sum_{r=1}^n\left[3(rh)^2+2(rh)\right]=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left[3h^3\sum r^2+2h^2\sum r\right]\). Using the closed forms for \(\sum r\) and \(\sum r^2\), this gives \(3\cdot\dfrac13+2\cdot\dfrac12=1+1=2\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Split the sum term by term first — handle the \(x^2\) piece and the \(x\) piece separately, each with its own closed-form sum.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: Express \(\displaystyle\int_0^3 x^2\,dx\) as the limit of a sum, and evaluate it.
solution: With \(h=3/n\): \(\displaystyle\int_0^3x^2dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}h^3\sum_{r=1}^n r^2\). Substituting \(\sum r^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6\) and \(h=3/n\), the limit simplifies to \(9\), matching \(\left[\frac{x^3}3\right]_0^3=9\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Always cross-check your Riemann-sum answer against the direct antiderivative evaluation — they should match exactly.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_{-2}^{2} |x-1|\,dx \]
solution: Breakpoint at \(x=1\). Split: \(\displaystyle\int_{-2}^1(1-x)dx+\int_1^2(x-1)dx=\left[x-\frac{x^2}2\right]_{-2}^1+\left[\frac{x^2}2-x\right]_1^2=4.5+0.5=5\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Solve \(x-1=0\) to find the split point, then integrate \(1-x\) before it and \(x-1\) after — never integrate \(|x-1|\) as written.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^{2} |2x-3|\,dx \]
solution: Breakpoint at \(x=1.5\). Split: \(\displaystyle\int_0^{1.5}(3-2x)dx+\int_{1.5}^2(2x-3)dx=2.25+0.25=2.5\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: The breakpoint doesn't have to be a nice integer — solve \(2x-3=0\) exactly and split there regardless.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^3 \{x\}^2\,dx \]
solution: \(\{x\}\) resets to \(x-k\) on each interval \([k,k+1)\), so on each of the three unit intervals, \(\{x\}^2\) behaves exactly like \(x^2\) on \([0,1)\): \(\displaystyle\int_0^1x^2dx=\frac13\). With three identical intervals, the total is \(3\times\dfrac13=1\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\{x\}\) repeats its exact shape on every unit interval — compute the integral over one period and multiply by the number of periods.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_{-1}^{1} |x|^3\,dx \]
solution: Split at \(x=0\): \(\displaystyle\int_{-1}^0(-x)^3dx+\int_0^1x^3dx=\int_{-1}^0-x^3dx+\int_0^1x^3dx=\frac14+\frac14=\frac12\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(|x|^3\) is even, so you could also double \(\int_0^1x^3dx\) directly — splitting explicitly is the safer default when you're not sure about parity.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^5 [x]\,dx \]
solution: Direct from the shortcut: \(\dfrac{n(n-1)}2\) with \(n=5\): \(\dfrac{5\cdot4}2=10\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: No need to split into five strips — the formula \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\) gives the answer in one step.

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^7 [x]\,dx \]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: This formula scales instantly to any integer upper limit — no extra work as \(n\) grows.

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^4 \{x\}\,dx \]
solution: \(\int_0^n\{x\}dx=\dfrac n2\) with \(n=4\): \(\dfrac42=2\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: The fractional part always averages to \(\tfrac12\) on each unit interval — multiply by the number of intervals.

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^{10} \{x\}\,dx \]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Same shortcut regardless of how large \(n\) is — the formula doesn't care.

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_2^6 [x]\,dx \]
solution: Use additivity to combine two applications of the shortcut: \(\displaystyle\int_2^6[x]dx=\int_0^6[x]dx-\int_0^2[x]dx=\frac{6\cdot5}2-\frac{2\cdot1}2=15-1=14\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: The \(\int_0^n[x]dx\) shortcut only starts at \(0\) — for a shifted interval, subtract two applications of it instead of re-deriving from scratch.

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_1^4 \frac{\sqrt{x-1}}{\sqrt{x-1}+\sqrt{4-x}}\,dx \]
solution: Here \(a=1,\,b=4\), so \(a+b-x=5-x\), and \(f(x)=\sqrt{x-1}\) gives \(f(a+b-x)=\sqrt{(5-x)-1}=\sqrt{4-x}\) — exactly the denominator's second term. So \(I=\dfrac{b-a}2=\dfrac{4-1}2=\dfrac32\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Check that the second term in the denominator really is \(f(a+b-x)\) for the same \(f\) in the numerator — that's what licenses the shortcut.

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^{10} \frac{\sin x}{\sin x+\sin(10-x)}\,dx \]
solution: With \(a=0,\,b=10\), the denominator is exactly \(f(x)+f(a+b-x)\) for \(f(x)=\sin x\). So \(I=\dfrac{b-a}2=\dfrac{10}2=5\), regardless of the fact that \(f\) is trigonometric rather than algebraic.
tip: 💡 Quick tip: This shortcut doesn't care what \(f\) actually is — algebraic, trigonometric, anything — only that the denominator has the right shape.
subject: math

question: \[ \int_0^{\infty} x^4 e^{-x}\,dx \]
solution: Direct from the Gamma shortcut: \(n!\) with \(n=4\): \(4!=24\).

question: \[ \int_0^{\infty} x^2 e^{-x}\,dx \]
solution: Direct from the Gamma shortcut: \(2!=2\).

question: \[ \int_0^{\infty} x^5 e^{-2x}\,dx \]

question: \[ \int_0^{\infty} x^3 e^{-x/3}\,dx \]

question: \[ \int_0^{\infty} x^7 e^{-x}\,dx \]

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^1 x^3(1-x)^2\,dx \]
solution: Direct from the Beta shortcut: \(\dfrac{3!\,2!}{6!}=\dfrac{6\times2}{720}=\dfrac1{60}\).

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^3 x\cos^5 x\,dx \]
solution: Direct from the Beta shortcut with \(m=3,\,n=5\): \(\dfrac12B(2,3)=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{1!\,2!}{4!}=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac2{24}=\dfrac1{24}\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: The half-integer arguments \(\tfrac{m+1}2,\tfrac{n+1}2\) become whole numbers exactly when \(m,n\) are both odd — that's when this shortcut is fastest.

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: \[ \int_0^1 x^4(1-x)^4\,dx \]
solution: Direct from the Beta shortcut: \(\dfrac{4!\,4!}{9!}=\dfrac{24\times24}{362880}=\dfrac1{630}\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Symmetric exponents like \(m=n=4\) still use the same formula — don't look for a shortcut-to-the-shortcut.

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: Find the average value of \(f(x)=\sin x\) on \([0,\pi]\).
solution: Average value \(=\dfrac1{\pi-0}\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\sin x\,dx=\dfrac1\pi\times2=\dfrac2\pi\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Compute the plain definite integral first, then divide by the interval length — don't try to combine the two steps.

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: Find the average value of \(f(x)=x^3\) on \([1,3]\).
solution: Average value \(=\dfrac1{3-1}\displaystyle\int_1^3x^3dx=\dfrac12\left[\frac{x^4}4\right]_1^3=\dfrac12\cdot\frac{81-1}4=\dfrac12\times20=10\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Watch the arithmetic on \(81-1=80\), not \(81-1=79\) — a common slip when the interval doesn't start at \(0\).
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: Given that \(2\le3+\sin x\le4\) on \([0,\pi]\), find bounds for \(\displaystyle\int_0^\pi(3+\sin x)\,dx\) without evaluating it exactly.
solution: Using \(m(b-a)\le\int_a^b f\,dx\le M(b-a)\) with \(m=2,\,M=4,\,b-a=\pi\): \(2\pi\le I\le4\pi\). (The exact value, \(3\pi+2\approx11.42\), does sit inside this range, between \(2\pi\approx6.28\) and \(4\pi\approx12.57\).)
tip: 💡 Quick tip: This technique estimates without evaluating — useful for sanity-checking an exact answer, or when an exact antiderivative isn't available.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: Find the average value of \(f(x)=e^x\) on \([0,2]\).
solution: Average value \(=\dfrac1{2-0}\displaystyle\int_0^2e^x\,dx=\dfrac12\left(e^2-1\right)\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\int e^xdx=e^x\) is one of the fastest antiderivatives available — the only real step here is dividing by the interval length.
subject: math

source: Practice question — for drill practice, not a past exam question
question: If \(F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^{x^3}\cos t\,dt\), find \(F'(1)\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Plug the upper limit into \(f\), then multiply by the derivative of that upper limit — here that's \(3x^2\) from \(x^3\).

question: If \(F(x)=\displaystyle\int_x^{5}\frac{dt}{1+t^2}\), find \(F'(2)\).
solution: Only the lower limit varies here, which contributes a negative sign: \(F'(x)=-\dfrac1{1+x^2}\). At \(x=2\): \(F'(2)=-\dfrac15\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: When only the lower limit is variable (upper limit constant), the derivative is just \(-f(\text{lower limit})\times(\text{lower limit})'\) — don't forget the minus sign.

question: If \(F(x)=\displaystyle\int_{\sin x}^{\cos x}e^t\,dt\), find \(F'(0)\).
solution: \(F'(x)=e^{\cos x}\cdot(-\sin x)-e^{\sin x}\cdot\cos x\). At \(x=0\): \(e^1\cdot0-e^0\cdot1=0-1=-1\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Both limits are moving here — differentiate the upper-limit term and the lower-limit term separately, then subtract as usual.

question: \[ \int_0^{\pi} \sin^2 x\,dx \]
solution: Using \(\sin^2x=\dfrac{1-\cos2x}2\): antiderivative is \(\dfrac x2-\dfrac{\sin2x}4\). Evaluating: \(\left(\dfrac\pi2-0\right)-(0-0)=\dfrac\pi2\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\sin^2x\) and \(\cos^2x\) should always be rewritten via the double-angle identity before integrating — never integrated directly as squared terms.

question: \[ \int_0^{\pi/4} \cos^2 x\,dx \]
solution: Using \(\cos^2x=\dfrac{1+\cos2x}2\): antiderivative is \(\dfrac x2+\dfrac{\sin2x}4\). Evaluating at \(\pi/4\): \(\dfrac\pi8+\dfrac14\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\sin(2\cdot\pi/4)=\sin(\pi/2)=1\) — a common evaluation point worth recognizing on sight.

question: \[ \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin 3x\cos x\,dx \]
solution: Product-to-sum: \(\sin3x\cos x=\dfrac12\left[\sin4x+\sin2x\right]\). Antiderivative: \(-\dfrac{\cos4x}8-\dfrac{\cos2x}4\). Evaluating from \(0\) to \(\pi/2\): \(\left(-\dfrac{\cos2\pi}8-\dfrac{\cos\pi}4\right)-\left(-\dfrac18-\dfrac14\right)=\left(-\dfrac18+\dfrac14\right)-\left(-\dfrac38\right)=\dfrac18+\dfrac38=\dfrac12\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\sin A\cos B=\tfrac12[\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)]\) turns any product of sines and cosines into a sum of simple sines — always faster than by-parts for this shape.
